steps.message:
I need a signed disposition on the third steady-solve attempt for the Ocotillo desert-fire case (CFDME-2025-041) before Mulshi starts a fourth.  Date it 10/10/2025.

Tell me what the residual plateau in that run is: the frequency and period this plume should show, what the run showed, and how close they are as a percentage.  Then whether a steady solution exists for this problem, how the rest of the delivered setup stands against our standards, and what any non-conforming item should be.

Then the run I am authorizing, as I will run it: the time-control block with values, our reference dictionary governing any ceiling the standard leaves case-specific, at the largest write interval and shortest end time our standard allows here.  Set it against the time-control block Mulshi delivered: every entry that differs, with both values.  Also which mesh the attempt ran on and what our verification of it covers and what it does not, and what in the delivered case carries forward, with the inlet's defining settings.

Last, cost.  Solver wall clock for one case as authorized and for the full matrix, in hours and minutes, on the firm's projection basis.  Tell me whether that basis can be met for the run I am authorizing, on every condition it sets, what the time step and Courant margin behind it imply, and what the figure is worth if not.  Then what attempt 3 consumed, how that compares against one authorized case, and what of it, if anything, is usable downstream.

A Word technical note on our letterhead with the reviewer and stamp block and our stamp boundary language.  SI, units on every value, simulated time in seconds to two decimals, wall clock in hours and minutes, frequencies and periods to two decimals, write interval to four.

Save as /filesystem/CFDME-2025-041_transient_solve_disposition_revA.docx please.
I'll start by exploring the filesystem to understand what's available.

From: Marguerite Falk <mfalk@thecfdme.com>
To: Renata Ellsworth <rellsworth@thecfdme.com>
Cc: Gordon Selby <gselby@thecfdme.com>
Subject: RE: projecting matrix wall clock off the study runs
Date: Thu, 09 Oct 2025 18:05:00 -0700
Message-ID: <20251010010500.9c3f7b16@thecfdme.com>
In-Reply-To: <20251010002200.2e81da45@thecfdme.com>
References: <20251010002200.2e81da45@thecfdme.com>
X-Mailer: Microsoft Outlook 16.0
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: text/plain; charset="UTF-8"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit

Renata —

There is a convention and it is deliberately a plain one. Five points, in order,
because people get two of them wrong every time.

1. For a fixed mesh, a fixed solver stack and a fixed core count, we take solver
wall clock as linear in simulated physical time. You establish the rate from a run
of record on that grid — simulated seconds reached, divided by wall clock consumed
— and you multiply that rate into the physical duration the production case has to
cover. That is the entire method. We do not model per-time-step cost and we do not
try to predict how the adaptive time step will wander over the run; the measured
rate already carries all of that.

2. Take the rate from the grid the production case will actually run on. Do not
carry a rate from one grid to another. Cell count and the Courant-limited time step
both change between grids, they change in the same direction, and they do not
cancel. If somebody hands you a rate off the coarse grid because it is the
cheapest number in the file, that is a correct answer to a different question.

3. Quote it per case first, then multiply by the number of cases the governing
scope document actually procures. Within a matrix every case carries the same mesh
and the same required physical duration; only the inlet condition changes, and
changing the inlet does not move the cost. Do not discount for cases you expect to
restart from a neighbour — we have never made that stick.

4. The number is solver wall clock and nothing else. Exclude queue wait, exclude
staging, meshing and decomposition, exclude post-processing, and exclude cloud-burst
provisioning latency. Label it as solver wall clock where you report it, or someone
will read it as a delivery date.

5. Write the linear-scaling step into the assumptions section of whatever document
carries the number. It is a projection under a stated assumption, not a measurement,
and it has to read that way to a client and to me. I will fold this into the next
revision of the verification standard; until then it is firm practice and this note
is the record of it.

Nothing here is new. It is the same basis we used to price the Copperline batches.

Marguerite

THE CFD ME | Tucson, Arizona | CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows | rev 4 | Effective 08/15/2025


Document: CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4 Author of record: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director &
Reviewing Engineer Registration: Arizona PE #42798 Supersedes: rev 3 (effective 02/01/2024) Distribution:
Firm-internal. All engineers and contracted CFD personnel performing fire, plume, wildfire, cavity-wall, or
buoyant-flow work under the CFD ME name.


1. Purpose & Scope
This standard is the firm-internal governing document for every CFD analysis undertaken by The CFD ME that
involves combustion, fire-driven buoyancy, wildland or WUI fire behaviour, compartment fires, plume dispersion from
thermal sources, or conjugate heat transfer through fire-exposed building assemblies. It applies to work performed by
employees of the firm, by remote engineers under a CFD ME employment agreement, and to any CFD hours
procured from an outside laboratory or contract shop. Where a subcontracted case is delivered against a CFDME
project number, the deliverable is expected to conform to this standard on receipt; deviations must be identified in the
transmittal and corrected before the case enters the firm's verification queue.
The standard is normative. Sections use "shall" and "must" for mandatory provisions, "should" for recommended
practice, and "may" for permitted alternatives. Where this document differs from a general-purpose CFD reference or
from a client-supplied specification, this document governs firm work product; a client-driven deviation shall be
captured in writing under the change-order provisions of the applicable Statement of Work.
The scope of this rev 4 explicitly includes:
• Open-atmosphere fire and wildfire simulations under wind loading.
• Compartment and enclosure fire simulations.
• Multi-region conjugate heat transfer through building assemblies exposed to a design fire, including double-wythe
   and cavity-wall constructions.
• Verification of mesh and time-step resolution for large-eddy simulations (LES) of buoyant reacting flow.
• Validation of firm predictions against certified third-party fire-endurance testing.
The scope explicitly excludes non-reacting external aerodynamics, forced-ventilation HVAC problems below the
combustion threshold, and high-altitude compressible aerodynamics. Those regimes are governed by separate firm
standards and are called out in Section 7 of this document.

2. Regime Selection
Fire problems shall be classified by the ratio of the incident wind velocity to the buoyancy-driven plume velocity scale
before any solver is selected. The controlling non-dimensional group is the Froude number formed on the
characteristic fire diameter:
Fr = u_wind / sqrt(g·D)
where u_wind is the design wind speed at plume height, g is gravitational acceleration, and D is the
characteristic fire diameter (for a distributed source, the equivalent-area diameter of the LES sub-domain segment).
Three regimes are recognised:
1. Buoyancy-dominated (still-air) plume — Fr much less than 1. The plume rises vertically; wind is negligible.
This regime admits a still-air buoyant treatment. 2. Mixed convection - Fr of order one, i.e. u_wind
~ sqrt(g·D). Wind and buoyancy contribute comparable momentum. The plume tilts, entrainment is asymmetric,
and the puffing structure interacts with the incoming boundary layer. This regime must be solved as a wind-forced,
buoyancy-reacting problem using the full fire solver package of Section 3. Substituting a still-air buoyant plume
when wind is present is prohibited under this standard, regardless of how "small" the wind appears in comparison to
the flame length. 3. Momentum-dominated — Fr much greater than 1. Wind dominates. Buoyancy still matters for
flame tilt and for near-source combustion but the far-field plume behaves as a passive scalar in a shear flow.
The regime call shall be made and recorded in the case setup memo at project kickoff. For the firm's Sonoran Desert
WUI design envelope (20-ft winds of 5–12 m/s over fire diameters of order a few metres), the ratio is order one and
the regime is mixed convection; this call has been made once at the firm level and shall not be re-argued
 case-by-case within that envelope.
Where the site meteorology or fuel model places a case outside the envelope for which a regime call already exists,
the responsible engineer shall compute Fr, record the value in the setup memo, and select the regime from the
classification above. Reviewers shall reject any case in which the regime is not identified in writing before the solver is
chosen.

3. Fire Solver Package
For all cases in the mixed-convection or buoyancy-dominated regimes with combustion present, the firm shall use the
fireFoam solver family: a reacting, buoyant, low-Mach, large-eddy simulation solver derived from the OpenFOAM
reacting-flow codebase. rev 4 mandates the following solver stack and configuration.
3.1 Solver. The solver is fireFoam. It shall be built against the firm's supported OpenFOAM version and pulled from
the firm reference-case library rather than assembled from external sources at case start.
3.2 Wind inlet. The atmospheric wind boundary shall use atmBoundaryLayerInletVelocity with the site
roughness length, reference height, and reference velocity taken from the project's site meteorological pull. The
companion turbulence quantities (k, epsilon or omega as applicable to the SGS closure) shall use their matching
atmBoundaryLayer* boundary conditions so that the inlet profile is thermodynamically and turbulently
self-consistent. Uniform-velocity inlets, plug flow, or synthetic-turbulence generators bolted onto a uniform inlet shall
not be used for open-atmosphere fire cases.
3.3 Combustion model. The combustion closure shall be EDC combustion — the Eddy Dissipation Concept, in the
finite-rate variant that couples the mean chemistry to the sub-grid strain-rate. Infinitely-fast Arrhenius,
mixture-fraction-only, and non-reacting passive-scalar surrogates for the fire shall not be substituted.
3.4 Radiation model. The radiation closure shall be fvDOM, the finite-volume Discrete Ordinates Method, with the
number of angular directions and the wavelength banding chosen from the firm reference table for the fuel and flame
temperature range. The absorption/emission coefficients for participating media shall be set consistent with the
combustion product composition, not defaulted. Simple radiation models (P1, view-factor) shall not substitute for
fvDOM in cases where cavity or enclosure radiation participates in the heat balance.
3.5 Thermophysical properties. Fluid-region properties (species, transport, thermo) shall use the JANAF/NASA
polynomials shipped with the firm reference library. Solid-region properties (concrete, steel, gypsum, insulation,
printed masonry, and any purpose-built assembly material) shall be temperature-dependent: k, rho, and cp shall
each be entered as a temperature-tabulated function or a supported polynomial fit over the design temperature
range. Constant-property short-cuts for solid regions in fire cases are not permitted.
3.6 Forbidden substitutions. rev 4 explicitly forbids substituting a steady HVAC configuration (buoyantSimpleFoam
or any other steady RANS buoyant solver) for the fireFoam package in any case in scope of this standard. The
steady HVAC solver family is validated for interior building airflow at metre-per-second-scale velocities without
combustion or radiation; it is not a permissible starting point for fire work.

4. Transient Behaviour and Time-Step Control
Buoyant fire plumes are not stationary flows. The plume necks, sheds, and re-forms at a characteristic frequency that
depends only on the fire diameter and gravity. The empirical Cetegen–Ahmed relationship, adopted by the firm as
normative for design fires in the buoyancy-dominated and mixed-convection regimes, gives the puffing frequency as
f = 1.5 · D^(-1/2) Hz
with D in metres. This is a physical property of the plume, not a numerical artefact.
Worked example. For a firm-standard LES sub-domain segment of D = 3.0 m, the puffing frequency is
f = 1.5 · (3.0)^(-1/2) = 0.87 Hz
corresponding to a puffing period of approximately 1.15 s. Every LES run at this diameter shall be expected to display
monitor-point oscillation at this frequency; that oscillation is the signature of physically-resolved plume dynamics.
No time-invariant resolution. Because the plume oscillates at a finite, deterministic, physical frequency, no
time-invariant flow field exists that any residual-tolerance schedule can converge to.
Time-step control. Transient LES shall use adaptive time-stepping keyed to the Courant number. The following
controlDict entries are mandatory:
 • application fireFoam;
• adjustTimeStep yes;
• maxCo 0.9;
• maxDeltaT <case-specific ceiling, typically 0.01 s>;
• writeControl adjustableRunTime;
• writeInterval <chosen so that at least 25 samples per puffing period are captured on
   monitors>;
The writeControl adjustableRunTime setting is required so that write intervals are pegged to wall-clock time
in the simulation rather than to solver iteration count, which permits the puffing signal to be sampled at a uniform rate.
Simulated end times shall span a minimum of 20 puffing periods after the initial transient has cleared, so that
averages, spectra, and RMS quantities are formed on a statistically meaningful window. For a 3.0 m fire that is a
simulated interval of no less than approximately 23 seconds of physical time, exclusive of startup.

5. Turbulence Modeling
The turbulence closure for cases in scope of this standard is large-eddy simulation. The sub-grid-scale (SGS) closure
shall be either:
• Dynamic Smagorinsky — with the standard Germano–Lilly dynamic procedure and a firm-default test-filter width
   of twice the mesh spacing; or
• WALE (Wall-Adapting Local Eddy-viscosity) — preferred where solid boundaries carry a significant fraction of
   the thermal load, because WALE returns the correct near-wall scaling of the SGS viscosity without requiring van
   Driest damping.
The choice between the two shall be recorded in the case setup memo. Static Smagorinsky with a hand-tuned
constant, k-epsilon variants applied to LES, and hybrid RANS/LES formulations are not permitted under rev 4 for
cases in scope.
Wall functions at solid boundaries shall be the OpenFOAM standard high-Reynolds treatment appropriate to the SGS
closure and the local y+ range. The mesh at solid walls shall be sized so that the first-cell y+ stays within the
recommended band for the chosen wall function across the design range of the flow, and this shall be verified after
the initial transient by inspection of the wall-shear field.

6. Multi-Region Conjugate Heat Transfer for Cavity-Wall Assemblies
Fire-exposed building assemblies in the firm's project portfolio are commonly double-wythe (double-leaf) cavity
constructions with a solid outer leaf, an internal air cavity, and a solid inner leaf. The two leaves are typically
connected by discrete metallic ties (galvanized-steel truss ties or comparable) at regular vertical spacing, embedded
some distance into each leaf. These ties are a metallic thermal bridge across the assembly and, in ASTM E119
practice, they set the single-point temperature-rise criterion.
For any such assembly under a design fire, the CFD case shall be a multi-region conjugate heat transfer setup,
not a single-region simulation with lumped-wall boundary conditions. The following region topology is mandatory:
1. Outer leaf — solid region. Temperature-dependent k, rho, cp per the firm concrete table. Cell size at the
fire-exposed face fine enough to resolve the thermal boundary layer. 2. Cavity — fluid region with participating
radiation. Air properties temperature-dependent; radiation solved with fvDOM as in Section 3; cavity emissivities set
from the firm assembly library. 3. Inner leaf — solid region. Same treatment as the outer leaf. 4. Ties — each metallic
tie is a separate solid region, geometrically embedded through both leaves and terminating in the cavity air. Ties are
not represented as a smeared conductivity on the leaf regions and are not omitted. Steel k, rho, cp are
temperature-dependent over the design temperature range.
Region-to-region coupling at every solid–solid and solid–fluid interface shall use the OpenFOAM chtMultiRegion*
coupled boundary conditions with matched temperature and heat flux across the interface. Contact resistance at
tie-concrete embedments shall be applied when a firm-approved value is available; where no value is available,
perfect thermal contact is the conservative default for single-point temperature-rise prediction.
 Mesh refinement. Refinement zones shall be defined at every tie–concrete interface, so that the concentrated
conduction into the tie is captured with cell dimensions at least a factor of four finer than the bulk leaf mesh at the
embedment. Failure to refine at tie–concrete interfaces has been observed in past casework to underpredict the
single-point temperature rise and thereby to overpredict endurance; rev 4 mandates the refinement to eliminate that
failure mode.

7. Cross-Regime Transfer
Validated status attaches to a case within an envelope, not to a directory. A case is validated for the physical
regime, the boundary conditions, the fuel model, the geometry, and the solver package under which it was verified
against a reference. Copying the case directory to a new project and changing the geometry does not carry the
validation with the copy.
Geometry and mesh topology are regime-independent: a well-formed hexahedral mesh of a printed-concrete wall
assembly is a well-formed mesh whether the outer boundary condition is a fire, a wind load, or a room-air HVAC inlet.
Physics, however, is regime-dependent. When the regime changes, the following shall be rebuilt from first principles
and not carried across:
• Freestream and inlet conditions (wind speed, direction, roughness, ambient temperature, humidity).
• Solver selection (fireFoam vs. non-reacting solver vs. steady HVAC solver vs. compressible aerodynamics
   solver).
• Combustion model (present with EDC, absent, or substituted per Section 3).
• Radiation model (fvDOM with participating media, absent, or reduced-order).
• Turbulence closure (LES SGS choice, RANS, hybrid — per the regime call).
• Thermophysical property treatment (temperature-dependent vs. constant).
Reuse is prohibited without full physics rebuild. In particular:
• A validated non-reacting external-aerodynamics case (e.g. from prior aerospace work) shall not be extended into
   a fire case by adding a heat-release term. The compressible non-reacting envelope does not overlap the
   reacting-buoyant envelope, and the freestream density, the inlet turbulence, the solver, and the closures all differ.
• A validated HVAC interior-building-airflow case (steady, low-velocity, no combustion, no radiation, adiabatic
   external walls) shall not be carried forward into any case in scope of this standard without a full physics rebuild.
   The HVAC envelope does not overlap the fire or plume regime; validated status in the former regime confers no
   validated status in the latter.
• A validated aerospace high-altitude compressible case shall not be pulled forward as the physics basis for a
   ground-level fire simulation.
Where a project geometry and a good mesh already exist from an earlier case in a different regime, they may be
retained and re-used; the physics on top of them shall be built new to this standard. Case-directory reuse without a
physics rebuild has been the root cause of firm rework in the past and rev 4 is explicit that it is not acceptable
practice.

8. Verification and Validation
Verification (numerical correctness of the solve) and validation (agreement with physical reference) are governed by
separate firm procedures and are not restated in full here.
• Mesh and time-step verification, LES resolution acceptance (D*/dx and Pope resolved-TKE tests), and the scope
   of applicability of Roache/Richardson grid-convergence-index methods shall follow the current revision of the firm
   QA Verification Standard — Mesh & Resolution. Engineers shall consult it before setting up any
   three-grid or resolution study; the scope statement in it governs which verification methods are permissible for
   LES versus for steady RANS work.
• Validation against physical reference - the E = S - D formulation, validation uncertainty u_val, and
   the firm acceptance criterion — shall follow the current revision of the firm Validation QA Procedure & Acceptance
   Criterion, which is itself aligned with ASME V&V 20. Certified third-party test reports are the required source
   of the reference value D; it governs the treatment of client-amended data.
 The verification and validation sections of any project report shall cite the current revision numbers of both standards in
force at the time the report is issued.

9. References
• OpenFOAM Foundation, OpenFOAM User Guide, chapters covering the fireFoam solver family,
   chtMultiRegionFoam conjugate heat transfer, atmBoundaryLayer* boundary conditions, and the fvDOM
   radiation model. Firm licence held; consulted for solver terminology and dictionary syntax.
• ASME V&V 20-2009, Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics and Heat Transfer.
   Invoked through firm document the Validation Procedure.
• ASTM E119, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials. Invoked through firm
   document the External Standards Digest, current revision.
• The CFD ME, QA Verification Standard — Mesh & Resolution rev 3.
• The CFD ME, Validation QA Procedure & Acceptance Criterion rev 2.
• The CFD ME, External Standards Digest , current revision.
• Cetegen, B. M., and Ahmed, T. A., Experiments on the periodic instability of buoyant plumes and pool fires,
   Combustion and Flame, source of the f = 1.5·D^(-1/2) correlation adopted in Section 4.

Issued by:
Marguerite Falk, PE Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer Arizona Professional Engineer #42798 The CFD
Mechanical Engineer, LLC 4820 E River Rd, Suite 220, Tucson, AZ 85718
Signed: M. Falk — 08/12/2025. Effective firm-wide 08/15/2025. Distribution: all engineering staff and contracted CFD
personnel. Filed under /Firm/Standards/.

Appendix A - Firm Reference Values (Sections 3.4 and 6)
The firm concrete table, firm assembly library, and firm reference table for the fuel and flame temperature range cited
in Sections 3.4 and 6 are reproduced below. Solid-region properties are held constant over the design range absent
case-specific data.
- Printed siliceous-aggregate concrete (outer/inner leaf): k = 1.4 W/(m*K), rho = 2200 kg/m3, cp = 900 J/(kg*K).
- Galvanized steel ties: k = 45 W/(m*K), rho = 7850 kg/m3, cp = 490 J/(kg*K).

Cavity emissivities (Section 6), grey diffuse:
- Concrete surfaces: 0.90 (matches the emissivity used in project reports).
- Galvanized steel tie surfaces: 0.25.

Radiation banding (Section 3.4, fvDOM):
- 4 angular directions (S4-equivalent quadrature).
- 2 wavelength bands, split at 2.5 micrometers, sized to the design fuel/flame temperature range of 1200-1700 K.

THE CFD ME | Tucson, Arizona | QA Verification Standard — Mesh & Resolution | rev 3 | Effective 07/01/2025

Document ID: CFDME-QA-VS-MR Revision: rev 3 Effective Date: 07/01/2025 Supersedes: rev 2 (Effective
03/15/2023) Author of Record: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer, AZ PE #42798
Applies To: All CFD deliverables issued from The CFD Mechanical Engineer, LLC (The CFD ME), 4820 E River Rd,
Suite 220, Tucson, AZ 85718


1. Purpose & Scope
This standard establishes the firm's minimum requirements for demonstrating that a CFD result is grid-independent
(for steady Reynolds-averaged work) or adequately resolved (for large-eddy simulation), and specifies how the
underlying evidence must be presented in the Verification section of every deliverable that leaves the firm.
The standard applies to every project executed by The CFD ME staff and to every subcontracted deliverable
prepared on the firm's behalf, including work performed by Mulshi Simulation Labs and any other external contractor
operating under a CFD ME work order. Reviewing Engineer sign-off on the peer-review checklist requires explicit
confirmation that the requirements of this document have been met.
Revision 3 rewrites the LES portion of the standard. The rev 2 language treated the Roache/Richardson grid
convergence index (GCI) as the default verification instrument for every solve regardless of turbulence treatment.
Two internal audits and a client peer review in Q1 2025 established that the treatment is technically incorrect for
large-eddy simulation and produces verification evidence that will not survive third-party scrutiny. The corrected
treatment is set out in Sections 4 and 5.
Nothing in this standard modifies the firm's Validation QA Procedure & Acceptance Criterion
(Firm/QA/CFDME_Validation_Procedure_rev2), the firm's Modeling Standards for Fire & Buoyant Flows
, current revision, or the Units and Conversions SOP
(Firm/Standards/CFDME_Units_SOP_rev2). Where the requirements of this standard intersect those documents, all of them
apply concurrently.

2. Definitions
Grid convergence index (GCI). A quantitative estimator of numerical uncertainty attributable to spatial discretisation
error, computed from a monotonic sequence of solutions on systematically refined grids under an assumed observed
order of accuracy. Reported as a percentage band on a selected integrated quantity of interest. The GCI is defined
for solutions that converge to a unique grid-independent limit as the mesh is refined.
Plume resolution index (D*/dx). The ratio of the characteristic plume diameter D* to the representative fire-region
cell edge length dx. D* is the buoyancy-driven length scale associated with a fire heat release rate Q_dot and is
defined as
D* = ( Q_dot / ( rho_inf · cp · T_inf · sqrt(g) ) )^{2/5}
where rho_inf, cp and T_inf are the ambient density, specific heat and absolute temperature respectively, and g is
gravitational acceleration. The index D*/dx is the standard measure of how many cells span the buoyancy-dominated
length scale of a fire plume.
Resolved turbulent kinetic energy (k_res). The turbulent kinetic energy carried by the explicitly resolved velocity
fluctuations in a large-eddy simulation, distinct from the sub-grid-scale contribution k_sgs modelled by the closure.
The resolved fraction is defined as k_res / (k_res + k_sgs).
RANS and steady work. In this document, "RANS and steady work" means Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes
simulations run to steady state, whether solved with a pseudo-time or true-steady solver, including internal buoyant
airflow of the type in the Copperline municipal HVAC envelope. Unsteady RANS (URANS) is treated as RANS for the
purposes of Section 4.
LES. Large-eddy simulation, including the firm's reacting-fire LES stack (fireFoam with EDC combustion and fvDOM
radiation) and any non-reacting LES of atmospheric or building flow.

3. General Requirements for Verification
Every deliverable that reports a CFD result shall contain a Verification section, plainly labelled as such, appearing in
the body of the report ahead of Validation and ahead of Results. The Verification section shall state, at minimum:
 (a) The turbulence treatment used (RANS, URANS, or LES) and, for LES, the sub-grid-scale closure.
(b) The representative cell edge length dx in the region of interest, and the total cell count.
(c) The verification basis chosen from Section 4 or Section 5, together with the numerical evidence supporting that
basis.
(d) A single-sentence statement identifying which acceptance criterion has been met and by what margin.
The Verification section shall not be an appendix pointer. Numerical values that support the verification claim shall
appear in the body. Supporting figures, residual histories, and mesh-slice imagery may be relegated to an appendix
and referenced.
Verification is prerequisite to Validation. A deliverable whose Verification section is absent, incomplete, or
inconsistent with this standard shall not be released for client transmission and shall not carry a Reviewing Engineer
signature.

4. Grid Convergence Index (GCI)
The Roache/Richardson grid convergence index is the firm's verification instrument for RANS and steady work only.
GCI is not valid for LES and shall not be used to verify any large-eddy result issued from this firm.
The reason is physical. Under systematic mesh refinement, an LES does not converge to a unique grid-independent
solution. As the filter width narrows, energy migrates from the modelled sub-grid-scale contribution into the explicitly
resolved field; the resolved-to-modelled turbulence split changes with the mesh. A three-grid sequence of LES
solutions therefore records a change in the physical content of the simulation between grids rather than a
discretisation-error tail collapsing toward a limit. The Richardson extrapolation on which the GCI is built assumes that
limit exists. It does not exist for LES, and therefore GCI values computed from an LES three-grid study are
numerically well-formed but physically meaningless. Non-monotonic behaviour in an LES three-grid quantity of
interest is the expected signature of the changing split, not evidence of a defective mesh study.
For RANS and steady solves, the firm applies the standard Richardson formulation. Given three systematically
refined grids with representative cell sizes h_1 < h_2 < h_3, refinement ratios r_21 = h_2 / h_1 and r_32 = h_3 / h_2
each at least 1.3, and a scalar quantity of interest phi with values phi_1, phi_2, phi_3 on the three grids, the observed
order of accuracy p is obtained from
phi_3 − phi_2 = ( r_32^p − 1 ) / ( r_21^p − 1 ) · ( phi_2 − phi_1 )
solved for p by fixed-point iteration. The fine-grid GCI on the finest pair is then
GCI_fine = F_s · | ( phi_2 − phi_1 ) / phi_1 | / ( r_21^p − 1 )
with a safety factor F_s of 1.25 when three or more grids are used. Reported GCI values shall carry the safety factor
and the observed p, and shall state the quantity of interest to which they apply. Monotonic convergence is a
precondition for reporting a GCI; oscillatory or divergent triples shall be flagged and the mesh study extended rather
than reported as a GCI band.
The requirement in this Section 4 applies without exception in the RANS envelope. Verification of a steady RANS
solve without a reported GCI (or an equivalent Roache/Richardson estimator) is not accepted.

5. LES Resolution Acceptance
For large-eddy simulations, the firm accepts either of the following as sufficient evidence that the resolution is
adequate in the fire or plume region of interest. Both are preferred; either alone is acceptable.
5.1 Plume resolution index. The plume resolution index D*/dx, computed with D* from the definition in Section 2 and
dx taken as the representative cell edge length across the buoyancy-dominated region, shall fall in the band 5 to 10.
Values below 5 are insufficient to carry the buoyancy-driven length scale; values above 10 are wasteful of compute
without corresponding gain in fidelity for the classes of fires the firm simulates. Q_dot in the D* expression is the fire
heat release rate applied in the LES, in watts.
5.2 Pope resolved-TKE criterion. The resolved turbulent kinetic energy shall be at least 80% of the total turbulent
kinetic energy in the region of interest, i.e.
k_res / ( k_res + k_sgs ) >= 0.8
 This is Pope's criterion for a well-resolved LES. The ratio shall be computed on a time-average of a statistically
converged solution window (typically ten or more integral time scales, or ten or more puffing cycles for a pool-fire-like
plume). Point probes shall be located within the buoyancy-dominated flow, not on the periphery of the domain.
Either criterion, met, is acceptable. Meeting both is preferred and is the default expectation for deliverables prepared
for authorities-having-jurisdiction or life-safety end use. Neither criterion may be evaded by asserting engineering
judgement in place of the numerical evidence; where a physical constraint prevents meeting either criterion, the
constraint and its consequence shall be stated explicitly in the Verification section and the deliverable escalated to
the Reviewing Engineer before release.

6. Reporting
The Verification section of every LES deliverable shall state, directly in the body of the report:
• The fire heat release rate Q_dot used to compute D*, with units.
• The characteristic plume diameter D*, with units.
• The representative cell edge length dx in the region of interest, with units.
• The plume resolution index D*/dx as a dimensionless number.
• The Pope resolved-TKE fraction k_res / (k_res + k_sgs) as a percentage, together with the location of the probe(s)
   and the length of the averaging window.
These values shall appear in the running text or in a table in the Verification section itself. Placement of any of these
values in an appendix, with only a cross-reference in the Verification section, does not satisfy this standard.
GCI values shall not appear in LES deliverables. A three-grid table copied forward from a RANS template into an
LES report, whether or not it is accompanied by a GCI band, is a non-compliant Verification section under this
standard. If a three-grid mesh study has been carried out on an LES case for information (for example, to
demonstrate insensitivity of an integrated quantity), the tabulated values may be included in an appendix labelled as
a sensitivity study, but they shall not be presented as verification evidence and no GCI shall be computed from them.
The Verification section of a RANS or steady deliverable shall state the observed order of accuracy p, the fine-grid
GCI on the reported quantity of interest with its safety factor, and the refinement ratios. D*/dx and Pope's criterion do
not apply to RANS deliverables and shall not be reported there.

7. Roles
Project Engineer. Responsible for constructing the mesh study or resolution assessment appropriate to the
turbulence treatment, computing the required indices, and drafting the Verification section in accordance with
Sections 3, 4, 5 and 6.
Reviewing Engineer. Responsible for confirming, on the peer-review checklist, that the Verification section of the
deliverable meets the requirements of this standard. The confirmation is a specific line item on the checklist and shall
not be a general "verification section reviewed" tick. For an LES deliverable, the Reviewing Engineer shall confirm
that D*, dx, D*/dx, and the Pope resolved-TKE fraction appear in the body of the report and that no GCI value has
been carried forward from a RANS template. For a RANS or steady deliverable, the Reviewing Engineer shall confirm
the presence of the observed order p, the GCI band and its safety factor, and monotonic convergence of the
underlying triple.
Owner / Principal Engineer. Retains final responsibility for the stamped CFD thermal analysis and for any release of
a deliverable in which the Reviewing Engineer has flagged a Verification-section deficiency that has not been
resolved.

8. References
1. Roache, P. J. (1994). Perspective: A Method for Uniform Reporting of Grid Refinement Studies. Journal of Fluids
Engineering, 116(3), 405–413. 2. Roache, P. J. (1997). Quantification of Uncertainty in Computational Fluid
Dynamics. Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics, 29, 123–160. 3. Richardson, L. F. (1911). The Approximate
Arithmetical Solution by Finite Differences of Physical Problems. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A,
210, 307–357. 4. Celik, I. B., Ghia, U., Roache, P. J., Freitas, C. J., Coleman, H., & Raad, P. E. (2008). Procedure for
Estimation and Reporting of Uncertainty Due to Discretization in CFD Applications. Journal of Fluids Engineering,
130(7), 078001. 5. Pope, S. B. (2000). Turbulent Flows. Cambridge University Press. (Chapter 13, resolved-TKE
 criterion for LES adequacy.) 6. Pope, S. B. (2004). Ten questions concerning the large-eddy simulation of turbulent
flows. New Journal of Physics, 6, 35. 7. McDermott, R., McGrattan, K., and Hostikka, S. (2008). Fire Dynamics
Simulator (FDS) Technical Reference Guide — Verification. NIST Special Publication 1018 (definition and use of the
plume resolution index D*/dx). 8. ASME V&V 20-2009 (R2016). Standard for Verification and Validation in
Computational Fluid Dynamics and Heat Transfer. 9. AIAA G-077-1998 (R2002). Guide for the Verification and
Validation of Computational Fluid Dynamics Simulations. 10. The CFD ME. CFD Modeling Standards — Fire &
Buoyant Flows, current revision. 11. The CFD ME. Validation QA
Procedure & Acceptance Criterion rev 2 (Firm/QA/CFDME_Validation_Procedure_rev2). 12. The CFD ME. External
Standards Digest, current revision.

Issued and signed:
Marguerite Falk, PE Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer The CFD Mechanical Engineer, LLC AZ PE #42798
07/01/2025

THE CFD ME | Tucson, Arizona | Validation QA Procedure — ASME V&V 20 | rev 2 | Effective 05/01/2025


Document: CFDME-QA-VAL-002 Author: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer (AZ PE
#42798) Supersedes: CFDME-QA-VAL-001 (rev 1, Effective 03/01/2024) Approved: Gordon Selby, PE — Owner &
Principal Engineer (AZ PE #48213)


1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure governs how validation is performed, evaluated, and reported for every deliverable of The CFD
Mechanical Engineer, LLC ("The CFD ME") that carries a validation claim. A validation claim is any statement,
quantitative or qualitative, that a simulation prediction reproduces a physical measurement within a stated tolerance.
Whenever such a claim is made — in a client report, a peer-review response, a testimony exhibit, or an internal
working record — the reasoning, arithmetic, and acceptance decision shall follow the steps set out here.
The scope covers all CFD analyses executed by staff engineers, remote engineers, and contracted vendors of the
firm, regardless of solver stack, regime, or client. It applies from the moment a validation reference is selected for a
project until the corresponding project file is closed and archived. Deviation from this procedure requires a written
waiver signed by both the reviewing engineer of record and the firm's owner, filed to the project's QA folder before the
deliverable is issued.
The procedure does not certify third-party test data, nor does it substitute for the engineering judgment of the
professional engineer of record. It fixes the form in which validation is expressed and the criterion against which it is
judged; it does not relieve any engineer of independent responsibility for the underlying analysis.

2. References
The following external standards inform this procedure. The firm holds single-user licenses to each; proprietary text is
not reproduced. The provisions relied upon are restated below in the firm's own words with citations back to the
source clause.
• ASME V&V 20-2009 (R2016), Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics
   and Heat Transfer. Framework for expressing validation as a comparison error with an associated validation
   uncertainty. See ASME V&V 20 Section 1 (validation framework and definitions) for the source
   formulation restated in Section 3 below, and Section 5 for the components combined in Section 4 below.
• ASTM E119-24, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials. Referenced
   for the exposure curve and the two thermal-transmission end-point criteria applied by testing laboratories. See
   ASTM E119 Section 8 (thermal transmission on the unexposed face · average rise and single-point) for the
   criteria whose interpretation is restated in Section 7.
• NIST NCSTAR 1-5 series, Fire Investigation of the World Trade Center Disaster, thermal-model validation
   appendices. Cited for community practice on uncertainty accounting in conjugate fire-thermal problems; not
   binding.
• Internal: CFD Modeling Standards - Fire & Buoyant Flows (M. Falk, PE); QA Verification Standard -
   Mesh & Resolution (M. Falk, PE); External Standards Digest (M. Falk, PE).

3. Model-Error Formulation
Validation shall be reported as the model error E = S - D with its validation uncertainty u_val, and never as a yes/no.
• S is the simulation prediction — the value produced by the CFD run using the model, mesh, solver, boundary
   conditions, and material properties documented in the report.
• D is the certified experimental value — the corresponding measurement produced by the physical test of record,
   drawn from the certified third-party report described in Section 6.
• E carries a sign. A positive E denotes a simulation that predicts more of the measured quantity than the test
   observed; a negative E, less. The sign is retained through every downstream comparison and is required in every
   rollup.
The equation E = S - D is the reporting form. Every deliverable that carries a validation claim shall present S, D, E,
and u_val in a single line or table, in that order, with a citation to the physical test report from which D is taken and to
 the run identifier from which S is taken. Descriptive words such as "matches," "agrees," "confirms," or "is validated"
are inadmissible substitutes for the numerical statement. The reviewing engineer shall reject any submitted
deliverable that omits any of the four quantities or that replaces the numerical rollup with a qualitative
characterization.
The requirement to report E with u_val — rather than a binary outcome — is not a matter of firm style. A yes/no
verdict conceals the sign and magnitude of the discrepancy, hides whether the disagreement is within measurement
scatter or resolved as a model error, and forecloses the diagnostic reasoning the validation exercise exists to support.
The reviewing engineer shall enforce the reporting form on every deliverable.

4. Uncertainty Build-Up
The validation uncertainty u_val is the root-sum-square (RSS) combination of three independent components, each
expressed in the units of the quantity being validated:
1. Numerical uncertainty, u_num. Reflects discretization, iterative convergence, and round-off contributions in S.
For the class of problem addressed in Section 8 — a conjugate thermal simulation of a compartment-wall assembly
under an ASTM E119 exposure — the firm's default value is ±4 min, established from prior three-grid conjugate
thermal studies on similar assemblies. A project-specific value shall be substituted where a resolution study or
convergence study supports one. 2. Input uncertainty, u_inp. Reflects propagation of uncertainties in material
properties (temperature-dependent conductivity, density, specific heat), boundary conditions (furnace-side
temperature histories, ambient side convective and radiative loss), and geometric idealization (leaf thickness, tie
diameter and spacing, cavity dimension). The firm's default value for the same class of problem is ±6 min. 3.
Experimental uncertainty, u_exp. Reflects instrument, calibration, and placement contributions to D as reported by
the testing laboratory. For calibrated Type-K thermocouples of the class used in ASTM E119 furnace work, the firm's
default value is ±5 min.
Combining by root-sum-square:
  u_val = sqrt( u_num^2 + u_inp^2 + u_exp^2 )
  = sqrt( 4^2 + 6^2 + 5^2 )
  = sqrt( 16 + 36 + 25 )
  = sqrt( 77 )
  = ±8.77 min
The result is reported to whole minutes: u_val = ±9 min for this class of problem.
Two guardrails apply.
First, the three components must be independent. If the numerical model uses lab-measured material properties
whose uncertainty is already folded into D, that property uncertainty shall not be double-counted in u_inp. The
reviewing engineer shall verify independence at the peer review stage.
Second, the default values shall be reviewed at least annually or whenever a project uses a materially different
assembly, exposure, or instrument class. A project-specific tabulation of u_num, u_inp, u_exp shall be recorded in
the project QA folder before u_val is published.

5. Acceptance Criterion
The firm acceptance criterion is |E| ≤ 10% of D.
The criterion is scaled: it grows with the endurance value being validated, so short endurances demand tighter
agreement in absolute minutes and long endurances tolerate more. A 30-minute endurance carries a 3-minute band;
a 120-minute endurance carries a 12-minute band; a 240-minute endurance carries a 24-minute band. This scaling is
deliberate. Absolute-minute criteria are unstable across the range of assemblies the firm analyzes; a 5-minute
absolute tolerance is loose against a 30-minute rating and severe against a 4-hour rating. A percentage-of-D criterion
is stable across the range and disciplines short-endurance work where the absolute stakes are largest.
Two secondary tests accompany the primary criterion and shall appear in every validation rollup:
• Compare |E| to u_val. If |E| ≤ u_val, the discrepancy is within the combined validation uncertainty and is best
   characterized as measurement-plus-model scatter. If |E| > u_val, the discrepancy is resolved as a model error —
   larger than the noise floor of the exercise — and shall be treated as an actionable finding, regardless of whether
    the primary 10% criterion is met.
• Compare the sign of E to the direction of the physical expectation. A simulation that consistently over-predicts
   endurance carries different engineering implications from one that consistently under-predicts; the sign is
   preserved in every rollup and discussed in the report narrative.
A deliverable in which |E| exceeds the criterion, or in which |E| exceeds u_val, or both, shall not be released with an
unqualified validation claim. The reviewing engineer determines whether the deliverable may be released with a
documented finding, whether the model shall be reworked, or whether the validation reference itself is unsuitable and
a different reference shall be sought.

6. Source of D
D shall be taken from the certified third-party test report of record. Client-amended values may not be
substituted for D absent a reissued report from the testing laboratory of record and a calibration certificate authorizing
the revision. Post-test amendments transmitted by the client but not authorized by the lab are not admissible as D.
The rule is strict for a reason. D is the physical anchor of the validation; if D moves for any reason other than a
documented laboratory action, the validation ceases to be against the physical test and becomes a comparison
against a preferred number. The two states are indistinguishable in the report if the substitution is silent, and the
record of the exercise is corrupted.
The following forms of documentation are required to substitute a revised D:
1. A reissued report from the testing laboratory of record, bearing the same report number as the original with an
amendment sequence (e.g., "-R1"), signed by the laboratory's authorized signatory, and stating the reason for the
revision. 2. A calibration certificate covering the instrument or measurement whose revision is at issue, with a date
and calibration-authority reference sufficient to trace the correction. 3. An explicit statement, in the reissued report,
that the revised value supersedes the value in the original report for all downstream use.
Absent any of the three, the original value stands. The reviewing engineer shall reject any deliverable that draws D
from a client-amended figure not backed by the above documentation. A polite, specific, thermocouple-calibration
explanation transmitted by a client is not a laboratory revision; the analyst shall record the client transmittal in the
correspondence folder and continue to use the certified D. Any pressure to depart from this rule — from schedule,
from commercial positioning, or from a persuasive account of what "really" happened at the test — shall be resolved
by returning to the reissued-report requirement.

7. Scope Limitation
ASTM E119 exposes an assembly to the standard building time-temperature curve, which is not a WUI
wildfire exposure. E119 endurance is therefore a comparative assembly rating, not a prediction of wildfire survival
time. Validation against E119 data validates the model against E119; it does not validate a wildfire performance
claim.
The distinction is not a formality. The E119 curve is a smooth, monotonically rising fuel-continuous compartment fire
scenario intended to grade the relative thermal performance of building assemblies under a repeatable exposure. A
wildland-urban interface exposure is a wind-driven, radiation-dominated, transient fire-front event whose peak heat
flux, duration, and spatial distribution differ from E119 at every axis. An assembly with a two-hour E119 rating is not
thereby a two-hour wildfire assembly, and no algebraic manipulation of an E119 result yields a wildfire survival time.
Firm practice on this point:
• Reports that use E119 test data to validate a CFD model shall state, in the validation section, that the validation
   exercise establishes model fidelity against the E119 exposure and shall not extrapolate that finding to wildfire,
   hydrocarbon-pool, or other non-E119 exposures.
• Where a project's ultimate objective is a wildfire performance claim, the validation section shall separately identify
   (i) what E119 data validates, (ii) what it does not, and (iii) what additional physical evidence would be required to
   close the gap.
• Marketing or commercial statements that translate an E119 rating into a wildfire performance figure are outside
   the firm's stamp and shall not appear in any firm-issued deliverable.

8. Worked Example — Illustrative Assembly
 The worked example below illustrates the arithmetic of Sections 3 through 5 using a hypothetical compartment-wall
assembly. The values used are illustrative and are not the values of record for any live project; they are pedagogic
only.
Inputs (illustrative).
• D = 120 min. Certified single-point endurance drawn from a hypothetical laboratory ASTM E119 report for the
   illustrative assembly. The single-point criterion governs per ASTM E119.
• S = 126 min. Simulation prediction from a conjugate CFD run mirroring the E119 furnace exposure for the same
   illustrative assembly.
• u_val = ±9 min. Per Section 4, using default values (u_num = ±4, u_inp = ±6, u_exp = ±5), combined by
   root-sum-square.
Rollup (illustrative).
• E = S − D = 126 − 120 = +6 min. Reported as E = +6 min, sign retained.
• Primary criterion: 0.10 × D = 0.10 × 120 = 12 min. Comparison: |E| = 6 min ≤ 12 min. The primary criterion is
   met.
• Secondary comparison to u_val: |E| = 6 min ≤ 9 min. The discrepancy is within the combined validation
   uncertainty.
Conclusion (illustrative). |E| = 6 min ≤ 12 min criterion AND ≤ 9 min u_val. The illustrative simulation would validate
against the illustrative certified test under the primary criterion, with the discrepancy sitting within the combined
validation uncertainty.
The point of the worked example is the arithmetic and the reporting form, not the outcome. In practice the analyst
reads D from the certified third-party report per Section 6, computes S from the run of record, tabulates u_val per
Section 4, and applies Section 5 to arrive at an acceptance decision. The engineering action that follows from a
non-validating rollup — grid resolution review, boundary-condition audit, material-property review, geometric
idealization audit — is not a substitution of D. Section 6 governs D.

9. Stamp Boundary
The CFD analyst of record stamps CFD thermal analysis only. The firm's stamp block on any deliverable that carries
a validation claim under this procedure shall read:
"CFD thermal analysis only. Fire-resistance rating certified separately by others."
Fire-resistance rating certification is reserved to the fire-protection professional engineer of record for the project.
Where the firm's CFD work supports a rating certification issued by a fire-protection PE, the firm's deliverable and the
fire-protection PE's certification remain separately stamped and separately scoped. A CFD validation finding under
this procedure is not a rating action; a rating action is not a CFD validation finding. Neither substitutes for the other,
and neither shall be represented as the other in any client-facing communication.

Document: Units and Conversions Standard Operating Procedure Revision: rev 2 Effective Date: 04/01/2025
Author / Owner: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer (AZ PE #42798) Applies to: All
engineering analyses, hand calculations, CFD case files, review checklists, memos, and reports produced by The
CFD Mechanical Engineer, LLC. Supersedes: Units and Conversions SOP rev 1.


1. Scope and General Principles
This procedure governs the units in which engineering quantities are computed, recorded, exchanged, and reported
at The CFD ME. It applies to every analyst and reviewer inside the firm, to every contracted CFD hour executed by
third parties on our behalf, and to every artifact — case files, logs, hand-calc worksheets, memos, and client
deliverables — that leaves any engineer's workstation.
The governing principles are three:
SI units shall be used internally throughout all analyses. Reports transmitted to clients working in US customary units
shall include a conversion table in report Section 1. Every numeric value in every artifact shall carry its unit in the
same cell or sentence — a bare number without unit is a defect.
The three principles are jointly binding. Internal SI discipline is not satisfied by a conversion applied at report time; it is
satisfied by keeping the analysis in SI from mesh generation through post-processing so that reviewers see a single
coherent unit system when they audit a case. The conversion table is not optional decoration; on projects whose
client-facing basis is US customary (ASCE 7 wind loads, ASHRAE inputs, Red Butte lab reports quoted in inches and
pounds), the table in Section 1 is the artifact the client uses to cross-read our numbers against their own, and its
absence is grounds for rejection at peer review. The unit-in-the-same-cell rule applies to spreadsheets, CSV column
headers, plot axis labels, memo text, and inline references — no exception is made for "obvious" units or for context
inherited from a section heading.

2. Preferred Units by Quantity
The following preferred units apply to all internal work. Deviations require written justification in the case-setup memo
and reviewer sign-off.

the unit adjacent to every numeric value.

3. Conversions in Routine Use
The following conversions arise routinely in this office's work — ASCE 7-22 wind-load extraction, ASHRAE HVAC
inputs, ASTM E119 lab reports, and construction-industry submittals. The values below are the firm-blessed
conversion factors and shall be used verbatim; do not re-derive from memory at the desk.
• 1 psf = 47.88 Pa
• 1 psi = 6895 Pa
• 1 lb (force) = 4.448 N
• 1 in = 25.4 mm
• 1 ft = 0.3048 m
• 1 BTU/hr·ft² = 3.155 W/m²
• 1 K = 1 °C (for temperature differences only; not for absolute temperatures)
• T[K] = T[°C] + 273.15 (for absolute temperature conversion)
Two of the above deserve emphasis. First, the psf-to-Pa factor is 47.88, not unity — a psf value carried into a Pa field
without applying the factor is off by nearly two orders of magnitude, which is precisely the failure mode this SOP
exists to prevent. Second, the temperature-difference identity (1 K = 1 °C) applies only to differences; a rise of 139 °C
is a rise of 139 K, but an absolute temperature of 139 °C is 412.15 K, not 139 K.
Additional conversions not listed above shall be sourced from the NIST SP 811 tables and cited by page in the
analyst's worksheet. Conversion factors quoted from web calculators, textbook back-covers, or LLM outputs shall not
be used.

4. Sanity Check Requirement
 Every reported field value shall be sanity-checked against the governing boundary conditions of the load case it
belongs to before rollup. Reviewers shall confirm this check on the peer-review checklist (item 9). A pressure reported
at a scale inconsistent with the case boundary conditions is a defect regardless of unit label.
The check is a scale check, not a unit check. A pressure field whose header reads "Pa" but whose values sit at a
magnitude the boundary conditions cannot produce is defective even if the string "Pa" is technically the intended unit;
the label alone does not vindicate the number. The check is performed at three points in the workflow: (a) by the
case-setup engineer immediately after the first converged or first fully-transient output is produced, (b) by the rollup
engineer at the moment values move from raw fields into summary tables, and (c) by the reviewer at peer review. The
reviewer's confirmation is recorded against item 9 of the peer-review checklist for that project.
Sanity checks are performed against the boundary conditions of the same load case. Cross-case checks are
governed separately by Section 5.

5. Cross-Case Cross-Checks
A structural wind-load case and a fire or plume exposure case on the same engagement are often
distinct load cases with pressure scales that differ substantially from one another. A value
reported from one case shall not be checked against the boundary conditions of the other.
This restriction exists because multiple load cases often coexist on the same project
and their pressure fields are stored in the same case-folder hierarchy. A reviewer who reaches for the wildfire
boundary conditions when sanity-checking a structural wind pressure — or vice versa — will incorrectly clear values
that belong to the other case, or incorrectly flag values that were correct all along. Each case has its own boundary
conditions and its own expected scale, and each is sanity-checked only against its own.
Where a report presents results from both cases, the report body shall separate them under clearly labeled
subheadings and shall not compute or narrate any ratio, difference, or combined figure that would imply a shared
basis.

6. Roles and Sign-Off
• Analyst (case-setup or rollup engineer): Responsible for enforcing SI-internal discipline at the case level,
   populating unit-bearing column headers and cell labels, and performing the Section 4 sanity check at case-output
   and rollup.
• Peer Reviewer (Technical Director or delegated PE): Responsible for confirming item 9 of the peer-review
   checklist against the artifact under review; responsible for flagging any unit-bearing defect as a report defect
   rather than an editorial comment.
• Principal Engineer (stamp holder): Responsible for confirming, prior to stamp, that the conversion table is
   present in report Section 1 when applicable, and that no bare-number defects remain in the deliverable.
• Technical Director: Owner of this SOP; responsible for periodic revision, incorporation of lessons learned from
   peer-review findings, and dissemination to contracted CFD hours executed on the firm's behalf.
Deviations from this SOP require written approval from the Technical Director in advance of the deviation, recorded in
the project folder.

    Purpose
    The firm holds current single-user licenses to the standards summarized below. This digest restates in the firm’s
    own words only the provisions the firm’s procedures rely on, with a citation back to the source clause. For any
    determination outside the summarized clauses, consult the source document. This digest may not be redistributed.
    The intent is to give firm engineers a quick, unambiguous reference to the specific clauses called out in our
    procedures (Modeling Standards, Verification Standard, Validation Procedure, Units SOP),
    without asking anyone to pull the full external standard for a routine check. Where a clause is quoted at all, it is
    paraphrased; no line of protected text is reproduced verbatim. Anyone needing the full text — for interpretation,
    for a determination outside the summarized clauses, or for any client-facing citation — must consult the licensed
    copy on the shared drive (see Section 5).

    1. ASTM E119 — Standard Test Method for Fire Tests of Building Construction and
    Materials
    Scope in firm use.
    ASTM E119 is the fire-endurance test method the firm’s assembly-rating work is anchored to. It is a laboratory
    test on a representative wall (or floor, roof, etc.) assembly exposed on one face to a controlled furnace fire that
    tracks the ASTM E119 standard building time-temperature curve.

    Standard fire exposure.
    The furnace follows the standard time-temperature curve: temperature rises rapidly in the first ten minutes and
    then continues on a defined logarithmic path (approximately 538 °C / 1000 °F at 5 minutes, 704 °C / 1300 °F at
    10 minutes, 843 °C / 1550 °F at 30 minutes, 927 °C / 1700 °F at 1 hour, and so on). The curve is a comparative
    fire exposure, not a representation of any specific real fire.

    Thermal-transmission criteria on the unexposed face.
    Two thermal-transmission criteria on the unexposed face of the assembly are monitored, both measured relative
    to the initial unexposed-face temperature at the start of the test:
           (1) Average unexposed-face temperature rise: 139 °C / 250 °F, measured as the arithmetic mean of nine
           thermocouples distributed on the unexposed face in accordance with the standard’s thermocouple placement
           pattern.
           (2) Single-point unexposed-face temperature rise: 181 °C / 325 °F, measured at any single thermocouple
           on the unexposed face.

    Governing endurance.

    The reported endurance for the thermal-transmission criterion is the elapsed time at which the earlier of the two
    criteria is reached. If the single-point criterion is reached before the average criterion, the single-point endurance
    governs; if the average criterion is reached first, the average governs. The reported endurance is not the later of
    the two, and is not any interpolation or average of the two.

    Practical note on cavity assemblies with metal ties.
    For a double-wythe cavity assembly with continuous metal ties (galvanized truss-type ties are typical), the tie
    forms a metallic thermal bridge between the exposed and unexposed leaves. In practice this frequently drives a
    single thermocouple sitting directly over a tie to reach the 181 °C single-point criterion before the average of the
    nine thermocouples reaches 139 °C. Engineers should expect the single-point criterion to govern in assemblies of
    that construction and should not treat that outcome as anomalous.
    Cite. ASTM E119 §7 (furnace control, thermocouple placement) and §8 (unexposed-face
    temperature criteria).

    What E119 is not.
    E119 is an assembly rating test conducted under a comparative standard fire exposure. It is not a wildfire
    exposure. It is not a natural fire, a compartment fire, a facade fire, or a wildland-urban interface fire exposure. See
    Section 4.

    2. ASME V&V 20 — Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid
    Dynamics and Heat Transfer
    Scope in firm use.
    ASME V&V 20 is the framework governing how the firm reports validation of a CFD model against
    experimental data. It is the basis of the firm’s Validation QA Procedure.

    The validation comparison.
    Validation is reported as the model error

                                                                       E = S−D
    where S is the simulation prediction (the model’s value for the validation quantity of interest, produced by the
    case as run), and D is the corresponding experimental data value (produced by a certified third-party test report;
    see §S6).      E is a signed number; it is not squared, not absolute-valued, and not otherwise normalized at this
    step.

    The validation uncertainty.
    The model error E is reported together with its validation uncertainty u_val. u_val is built as the
    root-sum-square of the numerical uncertainty component, the input uncertainty component, and the
    experimental uncertainty component:

                                                   u_val = √( u_num² + u_in² + u_D² )
    where u_num is the numerical uncertainty (discretization, iterative, and round-off contributions from the
    simulation), u_in is the input uncertainty (uncertainty in boundary conditions, material properties, and other
    inputs propagated through the model), and u_D is the experimental uncertainty (uncertainty of the measured data
    value D as reported by the testing laboratory).

    Reporting.

    Validation is reported as the pair E ± u_val, together with the comparison against the firm’s acceptance criterion.
    The reported form is never a bare “yes / no,” “pass / fail,” “validated / not validated,” or “within tolerance.” An
    engineer who cannot write down the three uncertainty components has not yet completed the validation and must
    not report a validation outcome.

    Comparison against acceptance criterion.
    The firm’s acceptance criterion is stated as a numerical bound on |E| (see §S5                for the current criterion,
    expressed as a percentage of D). The report states E, states u_val, states the criterion, and states the outcome of
    the comparison, in that order. If |E| is larger than both the criterion and u_val, the discrepancy is a resolved model
    error rather than measurement scatter, and that fact must be stated.
    Cite. ASME V&V 20 §1 (validation framework, definitions of S, D, E) and §5 (uncertainty estimation and combination).


    3. ASCE 7-22 — Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and
    Other Structures
    Scope in firm use.
    ASCE 7-22 governs the firm’s structural wind-load extraction work, including the Section 3.2 windward-wall
    pressure deliverables on projects that carry a separate structural wind case alongside a CFD scope.

    Velocity pressure.
    The velocity pressure at height z is computed as

                                                   q_z = 0.00256 · K_z · K_zt · K_e · V²
    with V in miles per hour and q_z in pounds per square foot (psf). The factors are:
         K_z — velocity pressure exposure coefficient, tabulated in ASCE 7-22 Table 26.10 as a function of height z
         above ground and Exposure Category (B, C, or D). For sites of the firm’s typical Sonoran Desert exposure
         (open terrain with scattered obstructions), Exposure C is applicable.
         K_zt — topographic factor from ASCE 7-22 §26.8. K_zt = 1.0 for essentially flat terrain (no isolated hill,
         ridge, or escarpment meeting the geometric thresholds of §26.8.1).
         K_e — ground elevation factor from ASCE 7-22 §26.9. ASCE 7-22 permits K_e = 1.0 to be used
         conservatively at all ground elevations; the tabulated value below unity may alternatively be used. Using
         K_e = 1.0 is conservative (higher q_z) at elevated sites.

    Note on K_d and where it is applied.
    In ASCE 7-22, the wind directionality factor K_d is applied in the design pressure equation, not in the velocity
    pressure equation. Do not multiply K_d into q_z. This is a change in equation form from earlier ASCE 7 revisions
    that some engineers may remember; check that any spreadsheet, template, or reference calculation reflects the
    7-22 placement.

    Windward wall design pressure.
    The design pressure on the windward wall is

                                                          p_w = q_z · G · C_p · K_d
    where:
         G — gust-effect factor from ASCE 7-22 §26.11. G = 0.85 is the default value for rigid buildings.

    4. ASTM E119 vs WUI — Interpretive Note
             E119 endurance is a comparative assembly rating under standard fire exposure. It is not a
             prediction of wildfire survival time. A validation against E119 data validates a model against
             E119, not against a wildfire performance claim.

    The distinction matters in practice because the same physical wall assembly may carry both an E119 endurance
    number (in minutes to the governing thermal-transmission criterion) and a separate CFD-derived wildfire
    exposure result (peak unexposed-face temperature under a Sonoran buffelgrass fire matrix, say). The two are
    answers to two different questions and may not be interchanged.
    Specifically:
         An E119 furnace fire follows the standard time-temperature curve. A wildfire, wildland-urban interface, or
         facade fire does not. Their radiative fluxes on the exposed face, their gas temperatures, their duration, and
         their variability in time are all different.
         An E119 test rates the assembly against a defined standard fire; the resulting endurance number is
         comparable across assemblies tested against the same standard. It is not portable to any specific real-world
         fire.
         A validation of a CFD model against E119 data establishes that the model reproduces the assembly’s
         behaviour under the standard E119 exposure, within the reported E ± u_val. It says nothing about the model’s
         accuracy under a wildfire boundary condition, which is a different physical regime.
    Statements of the form “the assembly survives a wildfire for X minutes” or “the model is validated for wildfire
    performance” are not supported by an E119 comparison alone and must not appear in a firm deliverable on the
    basis of an E119 validation. If the firm wishes to make a wildfire-performance claim, it must be validated against
    wildfire-relevant test data under the same framework in Section 2.

    5. License and Distribution Note

|    the parent template. Solver, turbulence, freestream, combustion and    |
|    radiation blocks are carried forward from the parent case. Geometry    |

|    site model.                                                             |

================================================================================
SECTION 1  --  SOLVER
================================================================================

  application            rhoSimpleFoam
  formulation            steady-state, pressure-based, compressible
  chemistry              none  (non-reacting)
  energy                 sensibleInternalEnergy
  compressible           yes
  transient              no

  Notes:
    rhoSimpleFoam carried forward from the Dry Wash Aerospace validated
    case. Steady, compressible, non-reacting formulation preserved.
    No reactive scalar transport is compiled into the solve.


================================================================================
SECTION 2  --  TURBULENCE
================================================================================

  simulationType         RAS
  RAS
  {
      RASModel                kOmegaSST
      turbulence              on
      printCoeffs             on
  }

  Wall treatment         standard wall functions on all no-slip surfaces
                         (kqRWallFunction / omegaWallFunction /
                          nutkWallFunction, per OpenFOAM defaults)

  Freestream turbulence  I = 0.5 %, mu_t/mu = 5   (inherited from parent
                         reference conditions of record)


================================================================================

================================================================================

  Reference pressure     p_inf   =  26,500 Pa
  Reference temperature  T_inf   =  223 K
  Reference density      rho_inf =  0.4 kg/m3
  Mach number            M_inf   =  0.25
  Reynolds regime        fully turbulent, wall-function resolved

  Notes:
    Freestream block inherited verbatim from the Dry Wash Aerospace
    parent case. The 0.4 kg/m3 reference density is the anchor value
    of the validated parent regime and has been retained here without
    modification.


================================================================================
SECTION 4  --  COMBUSTION MODEL  (NONE)
================================================================================

  combustionModel        none      // no combustion carried forward from parent
  chemistryModel         none
  reactions              (none)
  fvModels               (none active for chemistry or heat release)

  Notes:
    The parent Dry Wash case was non-reacting. No combustion model,
    no fuel source, no oxidizer transport, and no heat-release term
    are compiled into this case. The parent "no combustion" block is
    carried forward verbatim.


================================================================================
SECTION 5  --  RADIATION MODEL  (NONE)
================================================================================

  radiation              off
  radiationProperties    (dictionary intentionally omitted from constant/)

  Notes:
    The parent case carries no radiation participation. No
    radiationProperties dictionary and no radiative source terms in
    fvOptions are present. The parent "no radiation" block is carried
    forward verbatim. Wall surfaces are treated as adiabatic no-slip
    for the aerodynamics loads of interest.


================================================================================
SECTION 6  --  BOUNDARY CONDITIONS  (WALLS)
================================================================================

  Structure / ground / vegetation patch(es) [renamed to Ocotillo site model]:
      type               wall
      U                  fixedValue    (0 0 0)
      p                  zeroGradient
      T                  zeroGradient        // adiabatic
      k                  kqRWallFunction
      omega              omegaWallFunction
      nut                nutkWallFunction

  All wall surfaces use standard wall functions as declared in Section 2.
